5010:
When you call something or someone elite, you mean they are among the absolute best — not just good, not just great, but at the very top of their group. It describes people, things, or groups that have reached a level of excellence, skill, power, or quality that very few others can match.

Think of it as a kind of invisible filter. Imagine you take every soldier in the world and keep removing the ones who are slightly less skilled — you keep only the finest, the most capable, the most accomplished. The tiny group left standing at the end? Those are the elite soldiers.

The word carries two ideas together, always:

1. Exceptional quality or ability
Whatever is called elite is not just above average — it is at the very peak. An elite athlete doesn't just train hard; they perform at a level that puts them in the top fraction of a percent of all athletes on earth.

2. Exclusivity
Elite things and people are rare by definition. If everyone could reach that level, the word wouldn't apply anymore. There is always a sense of "very few make it here." Elite implies a narrow, high standard that most people or things simply don't meet.

These two ideas — exceptional quality + rarity — are the soul of the word. Whenever you see "elite," both ideas are present.
How It's Used in Different Areas of Life

The word "elite" travels across many areas of life. Here's how it works in each:

In the military:
An elite unit or elite forces refers to soldiers who are specially selected, exceptionally trained, and highly capable — far beyond regular troops. Think of special forces or navy SEALs. They are called elite because most soldiers cannot meet the extreme standards required to join them.

In sports:
An elite athlete is one who competes at the highest professional or world-class level. They are not just talented — they are among the best performers in their sport globally. A club-level tennis player is good. A national-level player is very good. A player competing for world titles is elite.

In education:
An elite university or elite school is one that has extremely high academic standards, admits very few students, and has a strong reputation for producing outstanding graduates. The selectivity and prestige are both part of what makes it "elite."

In society and social class:
The elite (as a group) refers to people who hold the most power, wealth, or social influence in a society — politicians, billionaires, top executives. When used as an adjective in this sense, something "elite" serves or belongs to this powerful group, such as an "elite social club."

In products and services:
An elite product, service, or membership refers to something of premium, top-tier quality — often expensive, exclusive, and designed to be better than everything else in its category.

It's important to understand that "elite" is a strong word. It is not just a fancy way of saying "good" or "excellent." There is a clear ladder here:

Decent → Good → Excellent → Outstanding → Elite

By the time you reach "elite," you are talking about a level that most people and things never reach. Using the word for something ordinary weakens it and sounds exaggerated. "Elite" should feel earned.
The Tone: Positive, But Sometimes Complicated

Most of the time, "elite" is used positively and admiringly. Calling a team, a skill, or a product "elite" is a genuine compliment — it signals the highest standard.

However, the word can sometimes carry a slightly complicated tone, depending on context:

When it sounds negative or unfair:
If people use "elite" to describe a group that has privilege and power, and that group uses that status to look down on others or keep others out, the word can sound critical. For example, "The elite schools only accept students from wealthy families" suggests something unfair and exclusive — not a compliment, but a criticism.

This negative feeling is often called elitism — the attitude that people or groups who are elite are somehow better as human beings, and that others deserve less. "Elitism" is almost always seen as a bad thing, even though being elite at a skill is generally admired. The difference is:

  • Being an elite surgeon (because of your exceptional skill) = admired
  • Being elitist (thinking you're a superior human being because of your status) = criticized

So the adjective "elite" is positive when it describes genuine excellence. It becomes complicated or critical when it's tied to unfairness, exclusion, or arrogance.

These are natural pairings with "elite" that you'll see and hear often:

  • Elite forces / elite troops — the most highly trained soldiers
  • Elite athlete / elite performer — someone at the peak of their sport or craft
  • Elite institution / elite university — a top-tier, highly selective school
  • Elite level — the highest standard of performance in any field
  • Elite club / elite circle — an exclusive group of highly powerful or accomplished people
  • Elite status — a special recognition given to top customers, members, or performers (commonly used in airlines, loyalty programs, etc.)
A Simple Test for Whether "Elite" Applies

Ask yourself three questions:

  1. Is this among the very best of its kind? (Not just good — the top.)
  2. Is it rare or hard to reach this level? (Can most people or things get here easily? If yes, it's probably not elite.)
  3. Would experts or people in the field agree it's at the top? (Is the standard real, or just self-proclaimed?)

If the answer to all three is yes, "elite" fits perfectly.

Elite describes something or someone that belongs to the very highest level of quality, skill, or status — exceptional enough to stand apart from almost everything else, and rare enough that not everyone can reach it.
5011:
The elite refers to a small, select group of people who are considered the best, most powerful, or most privileged within a larger group or society. The word always carries the idea of standing clearly above the rest — of being at the very top of some kind of ranking or hierarchy.

Think of it this way: if you have a country of millions of people, and only a tiny fraction of them hold the most wealth, power, or influence, that group is the elite.

For a group to be called "the elite," two things must almost always be true:

1. They are a minority. The elite is never the majority. It's a small, concentrated group. If everyone qualifies, the word loses its meaning entirely. The elite exists because most people don't belong to it.

2. They occupy the top. They are superior in some measurable way — whether that's wealth, power, skill, status, or influence. They're not just good. They're the best or most dominant in their domain.

"Elite" as a noun appears in a few forms:

"The elite" is the most common form. It refers to a group and is often treated as a plural noun, even though it looks singular.

"The elite control most of the nation's wealth."
"The elite have always resisted change."

"An elite" refers to one specific group that qualifies as elite within a particular field.

"The special forces are an elite within the military."

"Elites" refers to multiple such groups, often from different domains.

"Political elites and corporate elites often share the same interests."

The word isn't tied to just one area of life. It travels across many domains, and understanding these will sharpen your feel for it:

Social & Economic Elite — This is probably the most common use. It refers to the wealthiest, most privileged class in a society. These are people who were often born into money and status, or who accumulated so much wealth that they now exist in a completely different world from ordinary people.

"The social elite rarely interact with the working class."

Political Elite — Those who hold or influence government power — politicians, policymakers, advisors, and the networks around them.

"The political elite made decisions that affected millions, yet consulted almost no one."

Intellectual Elite — The brightest, most educated, most respected thinkers, academics, or experts in a field.

"The intellectual elite shaped the cultural conversation of the era."

Military Elite — The most highly trained, capable soldiers or units within an armed force.

"Only the most disciplined soldiers are admitted into the military elite."

Athletic or Sporting Elite — The very top performers in a sport, those competing at the highest levels.

"She trained for years before reaching the athletic elite."

The domain changes, but the core idea stays the same: a small group at the very top.
The Tone of the Word — Positive, Negative, or Neutral?

This is where the word gets interesting. "Elite" is not emotionally neutral — it carries different feelings depending on context and the speaker's point of view.

When used admiringly, it suggests excellence, discipline, and achievement. Calling soldiers or athletes "the elite" often carries respect — it means they've reached a level most people cannot.

When used critically, it suggests unfairness, arrogance, exclusivity, or being out of touch with ordinary people. Phrases like "the out-of-touch elite" or "the ruling elite" carry a sharp, resentful edge — the implication being that this group has too much power or privilege, and uses it selfishly.

When used neutrally, it's simply descriptive — the best in a given field, with no judgment attached.

So the same word can be a compliment, a criticism, or a plain fact — depending entirely on the sentence around it and the speaker's intent. Pay close attention to context.
The Hidden Idea Inside the Word

Here is something deeper worth understanding: the word "elite" only makes sense because of contrast. There can be no elite without a much larger group of ordinary or less powerful people below them. The elite are defined by the gap between themselves and everyone else.

This is why the word often appears in discussions about inequality, power, and fairness — because whenever there is an elite, there is, by definition, a majority who are not the elite. That tension is baked right into the word itself.

To sharpen the definition further, here's what the word does not mean:

  • It does not mean simply "good" or "skilled." A decent footballer is not part of the sporting elite. The word demands the highest tier.
  • It does not mean a large group. A group of thousands or millions cannot be "the elite" unless they are a small fraction of an even larger population.
  • It does not always mean deserving. Someone can be part of the elite purely through birth, inheritance, or corrupt power — not merit.

The elite = a small, exclusive group that sits at the top — of a society, an institution, a profession, or any human domain — by virtue of wealth, power, skill, status, or some combination of these. The word can be said with admiration, with resentment, or with plain description. But it always points to the same truth: these people are at the top, and most people are not.
5012:
Elitism is the belief or attitude that a small, select group of people — called "the elite" — are inherently superior to ordinary people, and therefore deserve more power, privilege, status, or influence over society.

The word comes from the idea of an "elite": a tiny group at the top, considered the best, the brightest, or the most powerful. Elitism is not just noticing that such a group exists. It is actively believing that this group deserves to be treated differently — that their opinions matter more, their choices should govern everyone, and that ordinary people are somehow less worthy.

Depending on the context, the "elite" might be defined by:

  • Wealth — the very rich
  • Education — graduates of the most prestigious universities
  • Social class — old aristocratic families, "high society"
  • Intellect — people considered exceptionally intelligent
  • Political power — rulers, top officials, influential networks
  • Cultural taste — people who appreciate "high" art, literature, or music

Elitism is the attitude that any one of these things makes a person fundamentally better than everyone else — and that society should be organized around serving, listening to, or being run by that group.
What Elitism Looks Like in Practice

It helps to see elitism across different areas of life:

Social elitism is the belief that people from wealthy or aristocratic backgrounds are simply better — more refined, more deserving of respect — than those from ordinary or working-class families. A person displaying social elitism might refuse to associate with someone because of their background, even if that person is kind, intelligent, and hardworking.

Intellectual elitism is the belief that highly educated or academically credentialed people should be the ones making decisions, and that the average person's opinion is too uninformed to be worth taking seriously. An intellectually elitist person might dismiss a farmer's or factory worker's political views as naive and not worth hearing, simply because that person doesn't hold a university degree.

Cultural elitism is the belief that certain forms of art, music, and literature — typically classical music, literary fiction, or fine art — are superior, and that people who enjoy popular culture, mainstream entertainment, or "lowbrow" media are less sophisticated or less intelligent. A cultural elitist might openly sneer at someone for enjoying a blockbuster film or a pop song, treating their tastes as a sign of a lesser mind.

Political elitism is the belief that a small class of experts, leaders, or powerful people should govern society, and that ordinary citizens are not capable of understanding or participating meaningfully in how the country is run.

Economic elitism is the belief that the wealthy have earned — and deserve to maintain — their dominant position in society, and that policies should be shaped to serve their interests, often at the expense of everyone else.
The Key Distinction: Elitism vs. Recognizing Excellence

This is one of the most important and subtle points about this word.

Not every preference for quality is elitism. A music school audition that selects only the most talented students is not necessarily elitist — it's selecting on merit. An editor who prefers a well-crafted novel over a sloppily written one is not automatically an elitist.

Elitism begins when you cross a specific line: when you start judging the person for their taste, background, or lack of credential — rather than simply evaluating the work or outcome. It also emerges when the criteria used to define "elite" are really about inherited privilege rather than genuine ability. A system that calls itself a meritocracy but in practice only rewards people who went to expensive schools, grew up in wealthy families, or have the "right" social connections — that is elitism dressed up as merit.

The crucial question is: Are people being judged on what they actually do and demonstrate, or on who they were born as and what advantages they started with? Elitism tends to confuse the two, treating the advantages of birth or privilege as if they were proof of genuine superiority.
Why Elitism Is Almost Always Criticized

In modern usage, calling something or someone "elitist" is almost always an accusation — and here's why:

It is unfair. Elitism typically justifies systems where some people have far more access to opportunities, resources, and power than others, not because of what they've earned, but because of who they are or where they were born.

It is exclusionary. Elitist attitudes and systems deliberately shut people out — from institutions, from conversations, from power — based on superficial markers like accent, background, credentials, or wealth.

It is arrogant. It assumes that certain people's views, experiences, and ways of living are inherently less valid or less interesting than those of the so-called elite — which is a failure of empathy and human recognition.

It often perpetuates itself. Elites tend to design institutions that favor people like themselves, making it harder for outsiders to break in, which reinforces the false impression that the elite's dominance is natural or deserved.
The Tone and Register of the Word

"Elitism" almost always carries a negative, critical tone. When someone says "that's elitism," they are usually charging the target with snobbery, arrogance, or unfairness. Even people who believe in the value of expertise or excellence will typically avoid calling their own views "elitist," because the word implies an unjust contempt for ordinary people.

You will hear the word used in political debates ("the elitism of the ruling class"), cultural commentary ("the elitism of the art world"), academic settings ("the elitism of Ivy League admissions"), and everyday conversation ("he's so elitist — he refuses to eat at any restaurant that isn't upscale").

Elitism is the belief that a select, superior group deserves more power, respect, and influence than ordinary people — simply by virtue of their wealth, education, class, intellect, or taste. It goes beyond recognizing genuine excellence: it involves looking down on those outside the group, treating their voices and choices as less valuable, and often defending systems that keep privilege concentrated in few hands. It is almost universally seen as unfair, arrogant, and exclusionary, because it substitutes inherited advantage or superficial status for actual human worth.
5013: When you call something or someone elitist, you are saying it reflects — or is shaped by — the belief that certain people are inherently superior to others and therefore deserve more power, privilege, access, or influence. It describes anything that favors an exclusive, select group while looking down on or shutting out everyone else.

At the heart of "elitist" is a specific worldview: that not everyone is equal in worth or deserving of the same opportunities. An elitist attitude holds that a special group — whether defined by wealth, education, family background, intelligence, social class, or taste — is simply better, and that this superiority gives them the right to more.

This isn't just about being part of an elite group. It's about believing that belonging to one entitles you to more — and that ordinary people deserve less, or don't really matter.
Who or What Can Be Described as "Elitist"?

The adjective is flexible — it can describe a person, an attitude, an institution, a policy, a system, or even a culture.

A person is elitist when they look down on others they consider beneath them, dismiss their opinions as unworthy, or treat ordinary people with condescension. They might refuse to engage with people who haven't gone to the "right" schools, or act as though only their kind of people are worth listening to.

An institution (a school, a club, an organization) is elitist when it is designed — formally or in practice — to serve, admit, or benefit only a privileged few, and excludes or sidelines everyone else.

A policy or system is elitist when it is structured in a way that keeps advantages concentrated among the already-privileged, making it harder for others to rise or participate equally.

A culture or environment is elitist when it makes people from ordinary backgrounds feel unwelcome, inadequate, or inferior — not because of anything they did, but because of who they are or where they come from.

• "The new school admission process is elitist — it basically filters out anyone who hasn't had expensive private tutoring."
  • "He can be really elitist about food. He refuses to eat at any restaurant that isn't award-winning and mocks people who enjoy simple meals."
  • "The conference had an elitist atmosphere — if you hadn't graduated from a top university, people barely acknowledged you."
  • "Her elitist attitude makes it impossible to work with her. She dismisses every idea that doesn't come from someone with an impressive title."
  • "Critics called the new arts funding policy elitist because it only gave money to prestigious institutions in wealthy neighbourhoods."
Why Is It Almost Always Used as Criticism?

The word carries a strongly negative connotation in most contexts. Here's why:

Most modern societies are built on the idea — at least in principle — that all people have equal worth and deserve equal opportunity. Elitism directly contradicts this. It says some people are more worthy by birth, background, or status. Calling something or someone "elitist" is essentially accusing them of being unfair, arrogant, and out of touch — of rigging the game in favour of a few while pretending the rules are neutral.

There's also an element of condescension baked into elitism. It's not just that elitists favour certain people — it's that they actively look down on others. That dismissiveness is what makes the label so cutting when applied to a person.

These two words are related but meaningfully different, and confusing them is a common mistake.

"Elite" simply means the best, the top, or the most skilled in a given area. A group of elite athletes, elite scientists, or elite soldiers are just exceptionally good at what they do. The word, on its own, has no moral charge — it's descriptive.

"Elitist", however, carries a value judgment. It introduces the idea of superiority giving someone a right to more — more power, more access, more respect — and often implies the accompanying attitude of looking down on others.

A surgeon can be elite (exceptionally skilled) without being elitist (arrogant and dismissive of others). But a surgeon who dismisses a patient's concerns because the patient isn't educated or important enough is being elitist.

The shift from "elite" to "elitist" is essentially the shift from being excellent to believing excellence makes you better as a person — and entitled to more.
One More Nuance: Descriptive vs. Critical Use

In rare, academic contexts, "elitist" can be used in a purely descriptive way — simply to say that something is associated with or designed for an elite group, without necessarily passing judgment. A researcher might describe a historical policy as "elitist in character" purely to categorise it.

But in everyday speech — which is how you'll encounter it 95% of the time — calling something or someone "elitist" is almost always a criticism. It's pointing out an unjust, arrogant, or exclusionary quality.

If you had to reduce it to its core: elitist describes anything shaped by the belief that certain people are superior and deserve more — and by extension, that everyone else deserves less or doesn't quite count.
5014: An elixir is a special liquid that is believed — or claimed — to have a powerful, almost magical effect on whoever drinks it. Think of it as a "wonder liquid." That core idea of a powerful, transformative liquid runs through every meaning of this word.

1. The Ancient, Mythical Meaning (Historical)

Long ago, people called alchemists spent their lives trying to discover two legendary substances. One of these was a liquid they called the elixir of life (sometimes called the elixir vitae).

They believed this elixir could:

  • Cure any disease or illness
  • Reverse the effects of aging
  • Grant the person who drank it eternal life (or at least an extraordinarily long one)

Of course, this liquid was never actually found — it was a myth, a dream. But the search for it consumed centuries of human imagination and effort. This is the original, classic meaning of the word.

"The old wizard spent his entire life brewing what he hoped was the elixir of life."

2. The Medical / Pharmacy Meaning

In real, practical medicine — especially in older times, but even today — an elixir refers to a sweetened, flavored liquid medicine. It is a solution where a drug or active ingredient is dissolved in a mixture of water and alcohol, then made pleasant to drink by adding sugar and flavor.

The key features of a pharmaceutical elixir:

  • It is always a clear liquid (not cloudy or thick)
  • It is sweetened to mask any bitter taste of the medicine
  • It contains alcohol as part of the solvent (the liquid that dissolves the medicine)
  • It is taken orally — meaning you drink it

A common example is children's cough syrup, which is often formulated as an elixir — a sweet, drinkable liquid with the medicine dissolved inside. Pharmacists still use this term formally today.

"The doctor prescribed an elixir that the child could swallow easily because it tasted like cherries."

3. The Figurative / Everyday Meaning

This is how you'll most often encounter the word in books, articles, and everyday speech. Here, elixir is used figuratively — meaning it is used poetically or loosely, not literally.

When someone calls something an elixir in this sense, they mean it is:

  • Highly effective at improving how you feel
  • Almost magically refreshing, healing, or energizing
  • The "secret ingredient" that fixes or transforms something

People use it to describe anything — a drink, an experience, a feeling — that seems to have an extraordinary, life-giving quality.

"After a long, exhausting hike, that cold water felt like an elixir."
"She always said that laughter was the true elixir for a broken heart."
"The coach's words of encouragement were an elixir for the team's low spirits."

Notice that in these examples, nothing is actually magic. The word is simply being used to say: "This felt incredibly powerful and transformative."
The Thread That Connects All Three Meanings

No matter which meaning is being used, an elixir always carries three qualities:

  1. It is a liquid — you drink it, or it flows.
  2. It is special — not ordinary, not plain. It has power.
  3. It transforms — it changes your state. It heals, restores, energizes, or fixes.

Whether it's a mythical potion granting eternal life, a carefully prepared medicine, or simply a glass of water after a desert hike — if something is called an elixir, the speaker is saying: "This liquid does something remarkable."

• Singular: "an elixir" — one specific magical or powerful liquid.
  • Plural: "elixirs" — multiple such liquids.

"The old alchemist had shelves full of elixirs, each promising a different miracle."
The Tone and Feel of the Word

This word carries a sense of magic, wonder, and power. It is not a neutral word. When a writer chooses "elixir" instead of just "liquid" or "drink," they are deliberately adding a feeling of mystery and special potency. It is slightly old-fashioned and poetic, which is exactly why it appears so often in fantasy novels, marketing for health products, and poetic writing.

If someone calls your grandmother's soup an elixir, they are paying it an extraordinary compliment — they're saying it heals the soul, not just the body.
5015: An ellipse is a closed, flat curve that resembles a stretched circle — like a circle that has been gently squished from two sides, or what people loosely call an "oval." It is a single, smooth, continuous loop with no corners or sharp edges.
The precise definition

Here is what makes an ellipse mathematically exact, not just visually approximate.

Start with two fixed points on a flat surface. These two points are called the foci (singular: focus). They sit inside the ellipse, one on each side of the center.

Now, pick any point on the edge of the ellipse — call it P. Measure the distance from P to the first focus, and the distance from P to the second focus. Add those two distances together.

The defining rule of an ellipse is this: no matter which point on the curve you pick, that sum of two distances is always the same constant number.

Move to a different point on the curve. The individual distances change — one gets longer, the other gets shorter — but their sum stays exactly the same.

This single rule completely defines the ellipse. In fact, it gives you a physical way to draw one: stick two pins into a flat surface, loop a piece of string around both pins (the string is the "constant sum"), pull the string taut with a pencil, and trace — you will draw a perfect ellipse.
The key parts

Center — the midpoint between the two foci. The entire ellipse is symmetric around this point, both horizontally and vertically.

Major axis — the longest straight line you can draw across the ellipse, passing through the center and both foci. Think of it as the "long diameter." Its two endpoints (where it meets the curve) are called the major vertices.

Minor axis — the shortest straight line across the ellipse, passing through the center, perpendicular to the major axis. Think of it as the "short diameter." Its two endpoints are called the minor vertices (or co-vertices).

Semi-major axis (a) — half of the major axis; the distance from the center to the far edge of the ellipse.

Semi-minor axis (b) — half of the minor axis; the distance from the center to the near edge of the ellipse.

Focal distance (c) — the distance from the center to either focus.

These three measurements are related by:

a² = b² + c²

This is essentially the Pythagorean theorem, and it holds for every ellipse.
How elongated is it? — Eccentricity

Not all ellipses look the same. Some are nearly circular; others are long and thin like a rugby ball. The degree of "stretchedness" is captured by a single number called eccentricity, written e:

e = c / a

(focal distance divided by semi-major axis)

  • e = 0: Both foci are at the same point — the center. The ellipse is a perfect circle. A circle is simply a special case of an ellipse.
  • e close to 0 (e.g., 0.1): The foci are close together. The ellipse looks nearly circular, just slightly squished.
  • e close to 1 (e.g., 0.95): The foci are far apart. The ellipse is very elongated and thin.
  • An ellipse always has 0 ≤ e < 1. Eccentricity can never reach 1 for an ellipse — at that point, the curve would open up into a parabola instead.
The standard equation

If an ellipse is centered at the origin of a coordinate plane, with its major axis along the horizontal direction, its equation is:

x²/a² + y²/b² = 1, where a > b > 0

Every point (x, y) that satisfies this equation lies on the ellipse.

If the major axis runs vertically instead, the a and b swap positions:

x²/b² + y²/a² = 1
Area and perimeter

The area enclosed by an ellipse is:

Area = π × a × b

When a = b = r (a circle), this becomes π*r*², the familiar circle area formula.

The perimeter of an ellipse, interestingly, has no simple exact formula. Unlike a circle, the perimeter of an ellipse cannot be expressed in a clean closed form — only through infinite series or numerical approximation. This is one of the famous "surprises" of ellipse geometry.
Ellipse as a conic section

An ellipse belongs to a family of curves called conic sections — shapes formed by slicing a double cone (two cones placed apex-to-apex, extending infinitely) with a flat plane.

Depending on how you tilt the plane:

  • Parallel to the base → circle
  • Tilted, but not enough to exit through the side → ellipse
  • Exactly parallel to one side of the cone → parabola
  • Steep enough to cut through both halves of the double cone → hyperbola

The ellipse (and circle) are the only conic sections that are closed curves — the others go on forever.
The reflective property

Ellipses have a beautiful physical property: any ray originating from one focus, when it strikes the inner surface of the ellipse, will always reflect directly toward the other focus.

This is not a coincidence — it is a direct consequence of the foci definition. This property makes ellipses extremely useful in optics, acoustics, and engineering.
Ellipse vs. oval

These words are often used interchangeably in everyday speech, but they mean different things.

An oval is an informal, non-mathematical term for any smooth, rounded, egg-like shape. It has no strict definition.

An ellipse is a mathematically exact shape, defined by the constant-sum property of its foci.

All ellipses are ovals, but not all ovals are ellipses. An egg, for instance, is not a true ellipse — it is wider at one end than the other, so it lacks the bilateral symmetry that every ellipse must have.
Real-world appearances

Planetary orbits — Kepler's First Law of planetary motion (1609) states that every planet orbits the Sun in an ellipse, with the Sun located at one of the two foci — not at the center. This was one of the most important discoveries in the history of science. The Earth's orbit has an eccentricity of about 0.017, so it is nearly circular, but slightly elliptical.

Whispering galleries — Rooms built with an elliptical ceiling or floor have the remarkable property that a whisper spoken at one focus is carried directly to the other focus and heard clearly, even across a large hall — entirely due to the reflective property of ellipses. The Statuary Hall in the U.S. Capitol is a well-known example.

Lithotripsy — A non-surgical medical procedure for breaking kidney stones. The patient is placed inside an ellipsoidal chamber so that the kidney stone sits at one focus. Sound waves generated at the other focus converge precisely on the stone and shatter it, without cutting the body.

Elliptical mirrors and reflectors — Used in optical instruments, headlamps, and telescopes to direct light from a source at one focus toward the other focus.

Satellite orbits — Many satellites orbit Earth in elliptical paths, with Earth at one focus. Highly elliptical orbits are used for some communication satellites to spend more time over specific regions.
Into three dimensions

When an ellipse is revolved around its major axis, the resulting three-dimensional solid is called a prolate spheroid (elongated, like a rugby ball). When revolved around its minor axis, it becomes an oblate spheroid (flattened, like a lens or a pumpkin).

The Earth itself is not a perfect sphere — it is an oblate spheroid, slightly bulging at the equator due to its rotation. Its equatorial radius is about 21 km greater than its polar radius.

A broader term for the 3D generalization is an ellipsoid, which is to a sphere what an ellipse is to a circle — a stretched version, with potentially three different radii along three axes.
In summary

An ellipse is a closed, smooth, oval-shaped curve defined by one precise rule: for every point on the curve, the sum of its distances to two fixed interior points (the foci) is always the same. A circle is its most symmetric special case. Its shape is governed by the relationship a² = b² + c², and its "stretchedness" is measured by eccentricity e = c/a, which always falls between 0 and 1. It appears as a conic section, carries a reflective property used in acoustics and optics, governs planetary motion, and extends naturally into three dimensions as an ellipsoid.
5016: Before anything else, here's the one idea that holds everything together: ellipsis means leaving something out. Both of its meanings — and it has two — grow from this single root idea. Keep that in mind, and everything else will make sense.
Meaning 1: The Punctuation Mark (the three dots)

An ellipsis is a punctuation mark that looks like this: ...

Three dots. That's it. But those three dots carry a lot of meaning depending on how and where they're used. Here are all the situations where you'll encounter them:

a) Cutting words out of a quotation

This is its most formal use. When you're quoting someone — from a book, a speech, an article — but you don't want to include every single word (because some parts aren't relevant), you use an ellipsis to show where you removed words.

Original text: "We must accept the good and the bad, the joy and the sorrow, and everything that life places before us."

With ellipsis: "We must accept the good and the bad...and everything that life places before us."

The reader sees the three dots and immediately understands: some words were removed here, but the meaning is preserved. It's an honest signal — it tells the reader, "I'm not showing you everything, but I'm not hiding it either. I'm just trimming."

This matters because it keeps quotations truthful. You're not allowed to just delete words silently; the ellipsis marks the gap openly.

One technical nuance worth knowing: Some formal style guides (used in academic or professional writing) place a period before the three dots when the omission happens at the end of a complete sentence, giving you four dots in total: .... The first dot is the sentence's period; the other three are the ellipsis. So if you ever see four dots in a formal piece of writing, that's what's happening.

b) A thought or sentence that trails off

In creative writing, fiction, and everyday communication, an ellipsis shows that a thought or sentence was started but never properly finished — it just fades out.

"I wanted to tell her the truth, but..."

The sentence doesn't end with a conclusion. It simply... dissolves. The reader feels the incompleteness, the hesitation, the words that went unsaid. This is one of the most expressive uses of the ellipsis.

c) A pause or hesitation

When a character in a story — or even a person speaking — pauses, hesitates, or is uncertain, an ellipsis can represent that beat of silence.

"Well... I suppose that could work."
"I'm not sure I... understand what you mean."

The ellipsis here mimics real speech. People don't always talk in smooth, unbroken sentences. They pause, gather their thoughts, or search for the right word. The three dots capture that human moment on the page.

d) Building suspense before a reveal

Writers sometimes use an ellipsis right before revealing something important, to make the reader hold their breath for just a moment.

"And the winner of this year's award is... Maria Chen."
"She opened the envelope slowly... and screamed."

The pause created by the ellipsis makes the reveal feel more dramatic.

e) Showing that time has passed

In storytelling, an ellipsis can bridge a gap in time — a signal that something has been skipped over and we're now further ahead.

"He closed his eyes. ...When he opened them, the room was empty."

f) In casual, everyday, and digital writing

This is where things get more informal. In text messages, emails, and social media, people use ellipses very freely — sometimes to connect thoughts casually, sometimes to let a sentence breathe, and sometimes to convey a tone that words alone don't quite capture.

"Sure... if that's what you want."

That ellipsis carries weight. It hints at doubt, reluctance, or even passive aggression. The meaning shifts depending on context and tone.

"I was thinking... maybe we could try that restaurant tonight?"

Here, the ellipsis is gentle and casual, mimicking a person thinking out loud.

This informal use doesn't follow the strict rules of formal writing. In everyday digital communication, people use ellipses to set a mood, a rhythm, or a tone — and that's perfectly fine in informal contexts, even if it would look sloppy in a formal essay.

Important things to know about the mark itself

  • An ellipsis is three dots — not two, not five, just three (with the exception of the four-dot variation explained above).
  • Some style guides write it with spaces between the dots: . . . — but the connected form ... is far more common.
  • It is treated as a single punctuation mark, even though it looks like three separate dots.
  • Never use it just to make writing look mysterious or to avoid finishing your thought in formal writing — that's poor style. In formal contexts, it has a job to do. In casual writing, norms are looser.
Meaning 2: The Grammatical Concept (leaving words out of a sentence)

This meaning lives in the world of grammar and linguistics. Here, ellipsis refers to the practice of leaving out words from a sentence because those words are already understood from context — so saying them again would be unnecessary and even awkward.

You do this constantly in everyday speech without thinking about it.

Full version: "Are you coming to the party?" → "I'd love to come to the party."
With ellipsis: "I'd love to." (The words "come to the party" are omitted.)

The listener already knows what "I'd love to" means. Saying the full version would feel robotic.

More examples:

"Who broke the lamp?" — "James." (Instead of: "James broke the lamp.")

"John can speak French, and Maria can too." (Instead of: "...Maria can speak French too.")

"She worked harder than he did." (Instead of: "...than he worked.")

In each case, the omitted words are mentally filled in by the listener or reader without any confusion. The sentence is shorter, more natural, and more efficient.

This is why ellipsis makes language powerful. Without it, communication would be exhausting — we'd repeat the same information over and over within a single conversation. Ellipsis is what allows us to be concise without being unclear.

They're not as separate as they might seem. Both meanings describe the same fundamental act: omission — leaving something out.

  • In Meaning 1, the three-dot mark is a visible, printed symbol that tells the reader: "Words were removed here."
  • In Meaning 2, it's a grammatical act: words are left out of a sentence because context makes them redundant.

In both cases, something is absent — but the absence is deliberate, purposeful, and understood. That's the heart of the word.

The plural of ellipsis is ellipses.

"The editor inserted an ellipsis to shorten the quote." (one)
"The passage contained several ellipses." (more than one)
One Word to Not Confuse It With

An ellipse (with no is at the end) is a completely different word. It refers to the oval shape you study in geometry. An ellipse is a shape; an ellipsis is a punctuation mark or a grammatical concept. They look and sound similar, but they have nothing to do with each other.

Ellipsis (punctuation)The three-dot mark (...) that signals omission, a pause, a trailing thought, or suspense
Ellipsis (grammar)The act of leaving words out of a sentence when context makes them obvious
Both meanings shareThe central idea of deliberate, understood omission
PluralEllipses
Don't confuse withEllipse (an oval shape)
5017: "Elliptical" has two distinct areas of meaning — one about shape, and one about language. Both come from the same root idea: something that is incomplete or leaves something out. Understanding both meanings fully will make this word click.

An ellipse is a geometric shape — think of a circle that has been gently squashed or stretched into an oval. It is a closed, smooth, curved shape with no corners.

When something is described as elliptical, it means it has this oval, elongated shape.

Examples:

  • The orbit of the Earth around the Sun is elliptical — not a perfect circle, but a slightly stretched oval path.
  • An elliptical machine at the gym is named for the smooth, oval path your feet trace while using it.
  • Some galaxies are described as elliptical galaxies — they look like glowing, smooth, football-shaped blobs rather than spiral discs.

The core idea: Elliptical = oval-shaped, like a squashed or stretched circle.
Meaning 2: Relating to language — leaving words out

This is where the word gets more interesting and subtle. In language, elliptical describes speech or writing where words have been deliberately left out, yet the meaning can still be understood from the surrounding context.

Grammarians call this device ellipsis — the omission of words that are understood but not stated.

Examples:

  • "She ordered the pasta, and he [ordered] the salad." → The word ordered is missing in the second part, but you understand it. The sentence is elliptical.
  • "Can you drive?" / "I can [drive]." → The word drive is dropped. The answer is elliptical — shorter than its full form, but perfectly clear.
  • "Some students passed the exam, and some [students] didn't [pass the exam]." → Three words are silently dropped. The sentence is elliptical but still complete in meaning.

The core idea: Elliptical = words are missing, but you can still understand the meaning from context.
Meaning 3: Deliberately vague, indirect, or hard to understand (an extended use)

This third meaning grows naturally out of Meaning 2. If leaving words out can make a sentence shorter and efficient, it can also make it obscure and confusing — especially when the speaker leaves out so much that the listener can't fully grasp what's being said.

So elliptical is also used to describe speech or writing that is indirect, cryptic, roundabout, or purposely unclear — where the speaker hints at things rather than stating them plainly, leaving the listener to fill in the gaps themselves.

Examples:

  • "The politician's answer was so elliptical that nobody could tell whether he supported the bill or not." → He spoke in a roundabout, evasive way, deliberately leaving out clear statements of his position.
  • "Her instructions were elliptical and frustrating — she kept alluding to what she wanted without ever saying it directly."
  • "The poet is known for writing in an elliptical style" → The poems hint, suggest, and imply — they don't state things plainly, forcing you to read between the lines.

The core idea: Elliptical = indirect or vague — leaving out so much that the full meaning is difficult to grasp.
How the two areas of meaning connect

Both the shape meaning and the language meanings share the same underlying logic: something is missing or incomplete.

  • An ellipse is a circle with something missing — it's not perfectly round, it's cut short in one direction.
  • An elliptical sentence has words missing — they've been cut out.
  • Elliptical speech has clarity missing — meaning is withheld or cut away.

Once you see this connecting thread, the word becomes very intuitive.

ContextWhat "elliptical" means
ShapeOval; like a stretched or squashed circle
GrammarWords left out, but meaning still understood
Communication styleIndirect, vague, or deliberately unclear
One sentence to remember it by
Elliptical means either oval-shaped (like a planet's orbit) or leaving something out — whether that's words in a sentence, or clarity in speech.
5018:
Elocution is the art and skill of speaking clearly, correctly, and expressively — especially in front of an audience. It is entirely about how you speak, not what you say.

Think of it this way: two people can say the exact same sentence, but one might mumble it quietly with a flat, lifeless tone, while the other delivers it with crisp clarity, perfect pacing, and a voice that commands the room. The second person has good elocution.

Elocution is not just one single thing — it is an umbrella term for several connected skills that together make a speaker sound polished and powerful. These include:

  • Clarity of speech — pronouncing every word fully and correctly so the listener doesn't have to struggle to understand you.
  • Voice control — managing the volume, depth, and quality of your voice so it sounds confident and pleasant.
  • Pace — knowing when to speak quickly to build energy, and when to slow down to let an important idea sink in.
  • Emphasis — stressing the right words in a sentence so your meaning lands exactly as intended. For example, notice how the meaning shifts: "I never said he stole it" vs. "I never said he stole it."
  • Tone and expression — matching the emotion and colour of your voice to what you're actually saying, so you don't sound robotic or monotone.
  • Pausing — using deliberate silences at the right moments, which gives your words weight and gives your audience time to absorb what you've said.
A Simple Way to Remember It

If what you say is your message, then elocution is your delivery. It is the packaging of your words. A gift wrapped beautifully gets more attention than one thrown in a torn bag — elocution is the art of wrapping your words beautifully.
Who Uses This Word, and in What Situations?

You will most often encounter the word "elocution" in these contexts:

  • Elocution lessons / classes — formal training sessions where a teacher helps someone improve the way they speak. These are common for actors, lawyers, politicians, newscasters, and anyone who speaks publicly for a living.
  • Elocution teacher / coach — a professional who trains people in the art of speaking well.
  • Elocution competition — an event (common in schools, especially in parts of South Asia, Africa, and Ireland) where students are judged on how well they recite a speech or poem aloud.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Since learners often confuse elocution with nearby words, here is a clear breakdown:

  • Diction is a narrower word — it usually refers specifically to the clarity of your pronunciation or your choice of words. Diction is one part of elocution.
  • Rhetoric is about the art of persuasion — crafting arguments and language to convince people. It focuses more on the logic and structure of what you say.
  • Oratory refers to formal, grand, and eloquent public speaking as a whole — think of a powerful political speech. Oratory is the result or performance, while elocution refers to the technical skills that make great oratory possible.
  • Eloquence means speaking beautifully and fluently in a way that moves people. You could say elocution is the training, and eloquence is the outcome.

So in short: elocution is the trained, technical skill set behind good speaking.

These will show you exactly how the word is used naturally:

  • "She enrolled in elocution classes before her first television appearance."
  • "His elocution was so precise that every word rang out clearly, even in the enormous auditorium."
  • "The drama school placed great importance on elocution, training students to control their breath, pace, and tone."
  • "Years of elocution training had given the lawyer a commanding presence in the courtroom."
  • "The students rehearsed for weeks ahead of the school's annual elocution competition."

Elocution matters because human beings respond not just to the words they hear, but to how those words are delivered. A well-spoken person comes across as more confident, more credible, and more engaging. Poor elocution — mumbling, rushing, swallowing words, speaking in a flat drone — can cause even brilliant ideas to fall flat. This is why elocution has historically been considered a mark of education and professionalism.
Elocution is the art of speaking clearly, expressively, and skillfully — it is the mastery of how your voice delivers your words to the world.
5019:
To elongate something means to make it longer — specifically, to stretch or extend it along its length so that it becomes more drawn out than it was before.

The reverse is also true: when something elongates on its own, it becomes longer, or it grows longer.

So elongate is about length increasing — either you cause it, or it just happens.

This verb works in two directions:

1. You do it to something (transitive):
You are the one causing the lengthening. Something is being stretched or extended by a force or action.

"The sculptor elongated the figure's neck to make it look elegant."
"The machine elongates the metal rod by pulling both ends."
"She elongated the vowel sound to make it easier to hear."

2. It happens on its own (intransitive):
Nothing is forcing it — the thing simply grows or becomes longer by itself, often naturally or gradually.

"The shadows elongate as the afternoon sun gets lower."
"During a stretch, the muscles elongate."
"The cells elongate as the plant grows upward toward the light."
The Key Nuance: It's Not Just "Getting Bigger"

This is important. Elongate is not about something growing in all directions. It is specifically about growing in one direction — lengthwise.

Think of a rubber band. When you pull it, it does not get wider or taller — it gets longer. That is elongation. The object is being extended along its longest axis.

Because of this, something that elongates often ends up looking:

  • More slender
  • More narrow
  • More stretched
  • Taller or longer relative to its width

A round lump of clay that a potter pulls upward elongates into a tall, narrow cylinder.
An artist who draws a person's legs longer than normal is elongating the figure.

Elongate carries a slightly formal or technical tone. You are more likely to see it in:

  • Scientific writing ("root cells elongate during growth")
  • Art and design ("the artist elongated the proportions")
  • Academic or careful descriptive writing

In casual conversation, people are more likely to say "stretch out" or "make it longer" — but elongate is the precise, single-word way to say the same thing with more accuracy and weight.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Several words are close in meaning, but each has a slightly different shade:

  • Lengthen — the most direct synonym. Neutral and general. Elongate often implies more of a visual stretching effect or a proportional change, while lengthen is simpler and more everyday. ("She lengthened the skirt by a few inches" vs. "The artist elongated the figure's limbs")
  • Stretch — implies pulling with physical tension or force, and sometimes the idea that it might spring back. Elongate is calmer and more permanent in feel.
  • Extend — broader in meaning. You can extend a deadline, a road, or a hand. Elongate is specifically about length in a physical or visual sense.
  • Prolong — used almost exclusively for time. ("She prolonged the meeting"). Elongate is rarely used for time.
  • Draw out — informal, and can mean either to physically lengthen or to make something take longer than needed.

While elongate is mainly a physical, literal word, it occasionally appears in figurative contexts:

"The speaker elongated each syllable for dramatic effect."
"The pause elongated uncomfortably before anyone spoke."

Here, it paints a picture of something being stretched — time, sound, a moment — beyond its natural or expected length. It creates a sense of tension or deliberate slowness.

You will frequently encounter elongate in these other forms:

  • Elongated (adjective) — describes something that has already been made longer or that appears stretched: "an elongated face," "an elongated shadow," "an elongated shape."
  • Elongation (noun) — the process or result of elongating: "the elongation of the spine during a stretch," "elongation of the metal under heat."
  • Elongating (present participle) — the ongoing action: "The shadows are elongating."

To elongate is to make something longer in a stretched, extended way — or for something to become longer on its own — with the change happening specifically along its length, often making it appear more slender or drawn out.
